profile.beat: A retail-facing swing-and-hold equity account (branded TLI) covering a concentrated book of small- and mid-cap growth names — AST SpaceMobile, Aduro, Hims & Hers, Zeta, Oscar Health, Gorilla, WYFI — alongside beaten-down large caps bought below their 200-week moving average (Alibaba, Sea, Novo Nordisk, UnitedHealth, Salesforce), plus Ethereum, Bitcoin and physical silver as hedges. It doubles as marketing for a paid subscription group, a YouTube channel and a futures-broker affiliate deal.
profile.style: Extremely high conviction, stated in absolutes: positions are 'moat goats', 'generational', in the 'Never Selling Category', and buys are 'all day long'. The analytical frame is Elliott wave counts plus Fibonacci retracements and, above all, the 200-week moving average, which he treats as a law — every fundamentally strong asset returns to it, so anything below it is a low-risk buy. Fundamentals appear mainly as free cash flow growth and insider buying used to confirm what the chart already said. Position sizing is discussed openly ('we went heavy', 'one of my largest positions', 'we typically make five buys per position') and drawdowns are reframed as market-maker raids or Citadel manipulation rather than as evidence against the thesis. Frequent scoreboarding of past winners, and open hostility toward other accounts, Cathie Wood, Bill Ackman, Jim Cramer and Michael Burry.
profile.cadence: Very high volume — roughly thirty posts a trading day, overwhelmingly short originals and quote-tweets of his own earlier charts, with running intraday commentary during earnings and Fed events. Recurring formats: annotated chart posts with named wave targets, 'Christmas Gift' annual picks, a Sunday $SPY chart, weekly publication schedules, valuation analyses and equity briefs teased on X and delivered inside the paid group, and list posts pairing tickers with a one-line thesis.
profile.revisits: Constantly, and it is the defining habit of the account — but almost always to mark a win. He re-quotes his own earlier charts to show a target hit (2085381219064127859, 2087903655722721371, 2095567562251669643), keeps a live scoreboard against Michael Burry's Nebius short (2087512252026867863, 2087645382142509522), and restates unchanged price targets months later (2094831469059310053, 2095431382709195038). Genuine changes of view are rarer but do exist: he flipped on SanDisk from expecting further downside to calling it attractive within two weeks (2082050611298672891 then 2082793679769473287), and moved the semiconductor complex from 'not yet' to a future buy list (2082102981609033871). Losses are acknowledged only in aggregate list form (2092962887924936842, 2095795886047551800).
profile.caveats: Substantial. (1) The account sells a subscription service, runs paid free-trial funnels and carries a paid futures-broker affiliate promotion (2075933320953663733, 2089674654898086114), so posts double as advertising and many calls are said to have been 'alerted in our group' before appearing on X — unverifiable from the feed. (2) Self-reported performance claims are unaudited and stated in absolute terms — a headline multi-year return figure for the account, and a claimed chart-accuracy rate he says is far above the industry norm — with no verifiable record behind either. (3) Entries are described retrospectively at flattering prices, and price targets are restated only where they worked. (4) Losers are minimised: the WYFI public offering that produced a large drawdown is reframed as an unforeseeable event rather than a thesis failure, and Nike and PayPal are dismissed in a single clause about weak management. (5) Drawdowns are systematically attributed to manipulation by Citadel and market makers rather than to being wrong. (6) He states he does not use stop losses and tells followers not to set them. (7) On Nebius he was posting targets and battling a public short while explicitly holding no position. (8) The tone is abusive toward critics, including a slur directed at a follower questioning the Gorilla chart (2092255234898735385).

narrative: The two months run on one organising idea: the US index is deep in a Wave 5 melt-up and a correction is coming in September, so the only safe places to be are assets that have already completed their own correction. From early July he repeats that parabolic moves are always met with proportionate declines, uses Micron and SanDisk as the live demonstration, and tells followers to avoid them, hold cash and add safe havens (silver, healthcare, China) instead of chasing. Through mid-July the market sold off hard and he treated it as a rehearsal — 'the market is testing you now for the real event from September' — and used the flush to add aggressively to AST SpaceMobile in the mid-fifties, Aduro, Alibaba below its 200-week average, Oscar and Hims. The last week of July was the pivot: he accused Citadel of manufacturing a rate-hike scare to force liquidations, said the Fed would not hike, and was proved right on the day, after which he claimed the July reset as a gift and went net long into August. August was a victory lap — Zeta, Oscar, Nebius, Salesforce, Alibaba and AST all rallied, he ran a public scoreboard against Michael Burry's Nebius short, and he insisted repeatedly that his names are 'not in the same cycle' as the index. His only real change of view in the window is tactical rather than directional: SanDisk moved from a short-side warning to 'looking even more attractive' once it reached the Fibonacci band on 30 July, and the semiconductor complex moved from 'BUT NOT YET' to a September shopping list. By mid-August he was explicit that he would 'be a Bear from September onwards' and forecast the index falling to its 200-week average over nine months, while simultaneously telling followers his own book would be exempt. The window ends with him repeating that the top is not in yet, that a September rate hike is the pivotal risk, and that the answer is to hold safe havens and names that have already corrected.

picks.prospect: Author expects Nvidia to keep running into its late-August earnings and to drag the market up with it, while warning that a reset will eventually come.
picks.risk_reward: He is two-sided here: he says the music will eventually stop and a reset will come as it did in 2025 even with strong fundamentals, but that it is not under threat while it holds its rising wedge and its support level. That support is the condition attached to the bullish view.
picks.thesis: Nvidia is the chart that determines the direction of the whole market; it historically runs into earnings, it held a crucial support level through the July weakness, and its margins are exceptional. He treats it as the market's key rather than as a value opportunity.

picks.prospect: Author expects Coinbase to break out of a tightening bullish wedge and reverse higher once it flips its 200 WMA to support, positioning it as the equity way to play a rotation into crypto.

picks.thesis: If crypto behaves like a safe haven over the coming months — which he argues is what it was designed for — the exchange benefits most from that rotation. Technically it sits below its 200 WMA after completing an ABC correction inside a bullish descending wedge.

picks.prospect: Author is waiting rather than holding: he tells followers to hold cash so they can buy Alphabet aggressively when its pull back completes, and says a portfolio should be built around it if the market gets irrational enough.
picks.risk_reward: He acknowledges the pull back he wants may not reach the level he named, which is why the call is conditional and cash-funded. He does not describe a loss scenario, only a missed one.
picks.thesis: Alphabet is one of the mega caps spending to catch what he calls the real AI boom, and he treats Buffett's average price as sitting in a suitable buy zone between Fibonacci levels. His rule is to buy quality only on a completed pull back, never on strength.
